items.title: Shadow IT
items.locator: Sections 'What is shadow IT?', 'What can you learn from shadow IT?' and 'Organisational mitigations'
items.quote: If you blame or punish staff, their peers will be reluctant to tell you about their own unsanctioned practices
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. Names shadow AI as a form of shadow IT, says it is rarely malicious, and advises a simple, quick request process, a no-blame approach and technical discovery (network scanning, cloud access security brokers). Version 1.0, published 27 July 2023, reviewed 14 August 2026.

items.title: ChatGPT and large language models: what's the risk?
items.locator: Section on whether queries are visible to the provider; recommendations
items.quote: not to include sensitive information in queries to public LLMs
items.why: The plain rule for staff: queries to public tools are visible to the provider and may be stored. A blog post from March 2023, so the description of particular products is dated; the advice stands.

items.title: AI and cyber security: what you need to know
items.locator: Section 'Questions to ask about the security of your organisation's AI systems'
items.quote: Do you understand where accountability and responsibility for AI/ML security sit in your organisation?
items.why: Written for board members and senior managers: the questions a board can put to its security staff. Does not deal with unapproved tools directly.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 32: Security of processing
items.quote: does not process them except on instructions from the controller
items.why: The binding rule behind an acceptable-use policy: the controller must take steps so that staff with access to personal data process it only on its instructions, and must keep security appropriate to the risk.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 28: Processor
items.quote: that is binding on the processor with regard to the controller
items.why: Personal data may be handed to an outside service only under a binding contract with sufficient guarantees. A free consumer tool that an employee signs up to personally will not normally have one with the employer.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Playbook for the UK Government
items.locator: Principle 3; section 'Public AI applications and web services'
items.quote: you cannot easily control the data input to the models
items.why: How government tells its own staff to treat public AI tools, and an example of a sanctioned-use framework (ten principles, used alongside each department's own policies). Written for the public sector.

items.title: AI adoption research
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Methodology (limitations); qualitative findings on responsible use
items.quote: Very few businesses said they had any internal guidelines or specific policies around using AI responsibly or ethically.
items.why: UK evidence that policies are rare, from qualitative interviews (no percentage is given). The report also states that, because it interviewed the person responsible for technology, 'the survey will not provide insights into shadow AI adoption'. Survey of 3,500 businesses by IFF Research and Technopolis; page updated 13 February 2026.

items.title: Trust, attitudes and use of artificial intelligence: A global study 2025
items.publisher: University of Melbourne and KPMG International
items.locator: Page 69 (PDF page 72); Figure 41 on page 71; executive summary (PDF page 8)
items.quote: The majority (70%) say they use publicly available AI tools that are free to use
items.why: Source of the figure. Survey of more than 48,000 people in 47 countries, including the UK; the figure is for employees who use AI at work and is not UK-specific. Also reports that almost half admit using AI in ways that contravene policy. Co-published by a professional services firm.

items.title: 2024 Work Trend Index Annual Report: AI at work is here. Now comes the hard part
items.locator: First finding, on employees bringing their own AI to work
items.quote: 78% of AI users are bringing their own AI tools to work
items.why: A second survey pointing the same way (31,000 people in 31 countries). Published by a vendor of workplace AI, so treat as indicative; not used as the brief's figure.

items.title: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank QPSC [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin)
items.publisher: High Court of Justice, King's Bench Division, Divisional Court (The National Archives, Find Case Law)
items.quote: Freely available generative artificial intelligence tools, trained on a large language model such as ChatGPT are not capable of conducting reliable legal research.
items.why: A UK court's finding on what happens when staff use free public AI tools unchecked: fictitious authorities were put before the court in two cases. The court said those with leadership responsibilities must take practical and effective measures so that everyone understands their obligations when using AI, and that it will ask whether they did. It makes acceptable-use rules a leadership duty. Limits: about lawyers and duties to the court; it does not address data leakage or tool approval in other sectors.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidance for Judicial Office Holders
items.locator: Section 3, part II 'Uphold confidentiality and privacy' (PDF page 5)
items.quote: Do not enter any information into a public AI chatbot that is not already in the public domain.
items.why: A model of a short acceptable-use rule written for the people who must follow it: what must never be entered into a public tool, the warning that anything entered 'should be seen as being published to all the world', and what to do after an accidental disclosure (report it as a data incident). Limits: written for judges and their staff in England and Wales; guidance; this version states that it replaces the April 2025 guidance, so it is revised often.

items.title: Risk Outlook report: The use of artificial intelligence in the legal market
items.quote: A staff member using an online AI, such as ChatGPT, to answer a question on a client's case.
items.why: A UK regulator naming unsanctioned staff use of a public tool as a specific threat to confidentiality and privilege, and telling firms they stay responsible for what the tools do. It shows how a regulator frames shadow AI for the firms it supervises. Limits: solicitors' firms in England and Wales only; a risk outlook, not rules; dated November 2023, and the SRA's site now also points to a later warning notice that was not read.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 24: Responsibility of the controller
items.quote: Those measures shall be reviewed and updated where necessary.
items.why: The legal root of an acceptable-use policy wherever personal data is involved: the controller must put in place organisational measures, including data protection policies where proportionate, be able to demonstrate compliance, and review and update them. The last point matches 'policy iterated on findings'. Limits: covers personal data only, not confidential business information or accuracy of output; it does not mention AI; 'where proportionate' leaves judgement to the organisation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Suggested action GV-3.2-003 under GOVERN 3.2 (PDF page 22); also GV-1.4-002 and GV-1.6-001
items.quote: acceptable use policies for GAI interfaces, modalities, and human-AI
items.why: International comparator. The United States standards body's generative AI profile lists as suggested actions defining acceptable use policies for generative AI interfaces, publishing transparent acceptable use policies, and enumerating the organisation's generative AI systems in its inventory: the policy and the visibility halves of this criterion. Limits: voluntary; United States; written for all organisations, with no detail on staff use of unapproved tools. The PDF text layer uses ligature characters in nearby words, so the quote is a clean fragment.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education
items.locator: Paragraph beginning 'Schools and colleges should also consider'; section 'Data privacy'
items.quote: there may be uses of generative AI by staff or pupils that have not been explicitly approved or adopted in their setting
items.why: UK government guidance that tells organisations to assume unapproved use exists and to plan for it: risk assessments 'should include plans for mitigating against unauthorised use cases', and personal data should not be put into generative AI tools. One of the few official UK texts to address unsanctioned use directly. Limits: schools and colleges in England only; departmental guidance, not law; the date is the 'Updated 12 August 2025' shown on the page.

items.title: From Frontier to Shadow AI: A Simmering Threat to Assurance and Security in Critical Infrastructure (arXiv preprint 2606.00088)
items.publisher: Mohan Baruwal Chhetri and others, CSIRO
items.quote: Drawing on semi-structured interviews with senior executives and functional leaders across 27 Australian CI organisations
items.why: The only empirical research found that studies shadow AI inside organisations instead of surveying individuals: interviews across 27 Australian critical infrastructure organisations, identifying three ways it weakens control (data leaving established boundaries, AI features embedded in existing software that nobody assessed, and loss of visibility for audit). Useful for what 'surfaced' has to cover. Limits: preprint, not peer reviewed; Australia; communications, energy and water sectors; qualitative, with no prevalence figure. The PDF text layer runs some words together.

items.title: The Adoption of ChatGPT (Becker Friedman Institute Working Paper No. 2024-50)
items.publisher: Anders Humlum and Emilie Vestergaard, University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute
items.quote: Workers report restrictions on use and needing training as the primary barriers to adoption
items.why: Large-sample evidence that employer policy, not worker reluctance, decides whether staff use these tools: in a survey of 100,000 Danish workers in 11 exposed occupations linked to register data, the main barriers reported were employer restrictions and lack of training. It supports the brief's point that guidance and a route to approved tools matter more than a ban. Limits: Denmark; one product; survey from late 2023 (the PDF is a revision dated 25 April 2025); working paper in this version; it does not measure unsanctioned use.
